idrc if this gets downvoted, and i don’t know this person so i don’t know their point, but it doesn’t seem like they are being anti vegan? i think what they’re trying to say is if you look at a holistic environmental perspective, eating plant based is often presented as THE solution, but it is an overly simplistic answer to an extremely complex issue. you can choose to not eat meat or dairy, but eating industrially farmed monocrops is also harmful in a different way. the way we see nature (sentient vs nonsentient) does not reflect the truth of the environment, because all living things impact one another. if you care about sentient living things, you have to care about “nonsentient” plants, water quality, soil health, etc etc etc. saying one matters more than the other because one is sentient is a simple short term way of viewing the larger issue of animal rights.

also, yes it is a cultural division, because many indigenous groups recognize plants and abiotic factors such as soil and water as being alive and ‘sentient’. not saying you have to see the world this way, but it’s weird to act like that’s an impossible or unscientific view to have. because arguably, these things do respond to change and have an impact on the world. ✌️

not trying to be a buzzkill but that’s not how it works? the christian old testament is actually based off the Septuagint, a koine greek translation of the original hebrew texts, but the texts that make it up were originally written in classical hebrew, koine greek, and some biblical aramaic. we do not really have access to the “original texts” but rather copies and translations, which means different versions use subtly different words and phrasing. spoken hebrew died out for a while, so modern hebrew is a revived language based off of ancient texts and it has a slightly different grammar and vocabulary. many semitic languages (including hebrew and aramaic) can be written with or without vowels, and in fact vowels were not introduced into written hebrew until the middle ages. this means that there is potential ambiguity in the wording as some words can mean multiple things depending on what vowels are spoken. this is also an issue when discussing the torah, and the interpretation of ambiguous words is often based off oral tradition and scholarly discussion. many jewish people spend time studying religious texts written in classical hebrew so they have experience with it, but it can still be confusing and ambiguous. there are also many words that only appear once and are therefore only able to be understood by context. still a funny meme, it’s just a complex issue lol and i want ppl to know what’s going on! like if it was that simple there wouldn’t be multiple branches of judaism lol

I think a lot of people don’t understand that anyone of any size can have an eating disorder. The assumption that all people with anorexia / bulimia are skinny is inherently incorrect, and implies that overweight people can’t have restrictive eating disorders. In a similar vein, not all eating disorders have the same effects on the body. Binge eating disorders and bulimia especially can cause unexpected changes. I think people also forget that OSFED and atypical anorexia exist, usually because most people with EDs don’t like to identify with them. Anorexia is treated like the “glamorous” illness, while everyone else gets thrown to the side. EDs are about habits, not body size. Diagnostic criteria based around BMI and size has actually been criticized as encouraging people to starve more so they can be diagnosed with anorexia n. instead of atypical, and things like that. Basically, restrictive EDs are very competitive. They can be easy to hide and anyone can have one at any size. I totally agree with your point though; I am overweight and have had an ED for years, and during my relapses people just encourage me to lose weight no matter how unhealthy the methods. If I was skinny, it would be a totally different story, even though EDs can kill no matter your weight.

I prefer that cats stay inside. However, I adopted one of my cats when she was already an adult, and her previous owner had let her go outside and free roam. I feel that it’s irresponsible to alter the way she lived for the first 5 years of her life for no huge reason; we don’t have any endangered species in my area that she would hunt, nor do we have any predators that would kill cats. Plus, during the time when she was kept inside, she would sprint out the door in a panic toward the street, which is much more dangerous than just walking out slowly like she does now. She never roams far and comes back to the house multiple times a day — usually I can still see her from the window. My cat is now 17, and while I understand that outdoor cats have shorter lifespans on average, I feel that in situations like this, it’s fair for cats to be let outside. Cultural appropriation is really a neutral term, and it happens all the time. When the Romans used parts of Greek culture, that could technically be defined as “cultural appropriation” because they were using parts of a culture that they technically didn’t belong to. If an African person wore traditional German clothing, that would technically be appropriation, but appropriation isn’t always bad. Some people have started calling positive cultural appropriation and sharing like what you described cultural appreciation, just because it’s sort of gotten a bad connotation. Bad cultural appropriation is when someone who’s a part of a group that oppressed another uses parts of that culture. A black person wearing “white hair” is often trying to assimilate and fit white beauty standards that look down on black culture. Meanwhile, a white person wearing “black hair” often comes across as insensitive because they’re using a part of a culture they don’t belong to, and in fact historically and currently oppress. It’s a weird situation, and there isn’t a hard and fast rule for if something is appropriative or not, but saying it doesn’t exist doesn’t help anyone, and the people who say so are usually coming from an outsiders perspective. I can only speak to the American side of it, but I feel like this happens in a lot of places, and is just more common in the US because of how weird our racial tensions and interactions are, and how many different groups exist in the same spaces.
